blocks.text: Ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy is one of the most popular analytical techniques because it is versatile and easy to use. UV-Vis light is passed through a sample and the transmittance of the light (T) is measured; the absorbance (A) is found from A = -log T. A UV-Vis spectrum shows the absorbance of a substance at different wavelengths, and the absorbance at any wavelength depends on the electronic structure of the molecule.

A compound can have sigma electrons (in sigma bonds), pi electrons (in unsaturated compounds only) and n electrons (non-bonding, lone pairs). Sigma bonding orbitals are lowest in energy, pi bonding orbitals higher, and non-bonding orbitals higher still. When radiation of the right frequency is absorbed, an electron moves from one of these orbitals to an empty anti-bonding orbital, sigma* or pi*. UV-Vis spectroscopy uses wavelengths of about 200-800 nm. The important transitions are pi to pi*, n to pi* and n to sigma*.

Buta-1,3-diene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2, absorbs most strongly at 217 nm; the wavelength of maximum absorption is called lambda max. This is in the UV region, so no visible light is absorbed and the compound is colourless. It has no non-bonding electrons, so the only transitions measured are pi to pi*.

Lambda max depends strongly on the extent of conjugation, as butadiene (217 nm), hexatriene (257 nm) and octatetraene (290 nm) show. In a conjugated system electrons are shared over a long chain; the more conjugated a compound, the more energy levels it has and the smaller the gaps between them. Smaller gaps need less energy, so light of lower frequency and longer wavelength is absorbed. Each extra conjugated double bond usually raises lambda max by about 30 to 40 nm, and highly conjugated compounds absorb visible light and are often brightly coloured.

blocks.alt: Top left: energy levels sigma, pi, n, pi* and sigma* from bottom to top, with arrows for sigma to sigma*, pi to pi*, n to sigma* and n to pi*. Top right: the absorption spectrum of buta-1,3-diene, a single peak at 217 nm between 200 and 300 nm. Bottom: butadiene (217 nm), hexatriene (257 nm) and octatetraene (290 nm) drawn as zigzag chains of alternating double and single bonds.
blocks.caption: Electronic transitions, the spectrum of butadiene and the effect of conjugation (original diagram after Figures 29.4 and 29.5).
blocks.long_description: The n to pi* jump is the smallest and sigma to sigma* the largest. In a conjugated chain the gap between the highest filled pi orbital and the lowest empty pi* orbital shrinks as the chain grows, so lambda max moves to longer wavelengths.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: A green tomato and a ripe red tomato have different colours: a green tomato has much chlorophyll, while a red tomato contains lycopene. The two compounds have different lambda max values and so specific colours in the visible range.

blocks.title: Colour of a complex from its spectrum
blocks.text: If a transition metal complex absorbs in part of the visible range, it appears the complementary colour (Chapter 18, colour wheel): a complex absorbing orange light looks blue.

blocks.prompt: Which of sigma to sigma*, pi to pi*, n to sigma* and n to pi* needs the least energy? Explain.
blocks.explanation: n to pi*: non-bonding electrons are the highest-energy filled orbitals and pi* is the lowest empty orbital, so this gap is the smallest.

blocks.prompt: Arrange in increasing lambda max: (i) CH3CH2-C(=CH2)-CH=CH-CO-CH3, (ii) CH2=CH-CO-CH3, (iii) CH2=CH-CH=CH-CO-CH3.
blocks.explanation: (ii) < (iii) < (i): (ii) has two conjugated double bonds (C=C and C=O); (iii) and (i) each have three; (i) also has an alkyl (ethyl) group on the conjugated chain, which shifts lambda max slightly further. (Structures read from the printed drawings.)

blocks.prompt: Will CH3CH(OH)CH3 show significant absorption in the UV-Vis region?
blocks.explanation: No: propan-2-ol has only sigma and n electrons; its sigma to sigma* and n to sigma* transitions need radiation below 200 nm, outside the 200-800 nm range.

items: A = -log T; UV-Vis uses about 200-800 nm.
Transitions: pi to pi*, n to pi*, n to sigma*; n to pi* needs least energy.
More conjugation: smaller gap, longer lambda max (217, 257, 290 nm).
